backTranslations.41: **Before the appointment** - Add the appointment date in the Appointment tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and how they can be made stronger. Choose the most important topics and questions; keep to three or four. Make notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date. **During the appointment** - Hand or show the first page to the doctor. It is made to be readable in under a minute: counts, averages, heat calendar and your questions. Start with the question most important to you. If your doctor speaks another language, you can make the notes in that language. **What the notes are and are not** They are a summary of the information you entered, plus whatever you chose to bring from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and any patterns shown in them are coincidence checks, not proof of cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal. **After the appointment** Add any new medication with its start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show you before-and-after entries, which makes your next review easier.
backTranslations.42: **Menopause** is a point in time: the day when 12 months in a row have passed with no period, and there is no other reason for it (such as pregnancy, certain medicines or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early fifties, but anywhere between about 45 and 55 is common. **Perimenopause** is the period of years before that point. Hormone levels go up and down unevenly, so periods can be irregular, heavier or lighter, more frequent or more spaced out. Many menopause-related changes, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often start here, while periods are still coming. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and it differs in everyone. **Postmenopause** is the whole time after that 12-month milestone. Some symptoms settle over time; some can continue for years. Menopause can also occur earlier, due to surgery removing the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is appropriate to talk to a doctor about this. **How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, doctors recognise perimenopause or menopause from your history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels change day to day. They are used more when the person is younger or the picture is unclear. **What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of your experiences: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162: Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of intense heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with skin reddening, sweating, a fast heartbeat or chills afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and it can be strong enough to wake you or soak the sheets. They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people get a few mild hot flashes; others get many in a day, disturbing work and sleep. In some people they reduce in a few years; in others they last a very long time. **What can make them more likely.** People often notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy bedding. These vary greatly between individuals, so tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list. **There are other causes.** Facial redness and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infections, some medicines, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell a doctor. **Describing them well.** Useful information for an appointment: roughly how many in the day and at night; how intense they feel and how long they last; what they interfere with: sleep, work, conversation, exercise; what usually happens before them; what you have tried, and whether it changed anything. MenoMap's wave button and the log for entering later are made to record exactly this information without much effort. **Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. Which are right for you is a matter for conversation with a doctor.

backTranslations.291: Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) makes up some of the estrogen that the body starts making less of around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people, and it can help with other symptoms too. **It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms like vaginal dryness. People who have a uterus are generally also given a progestogen along with estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus. **Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how long since periods stopped, personal and family history (such as breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type of treatment and how it is taken. This is why this decision should be made with a doctor who knows your history; an app cannot decide it. **Questions people often ask:** Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not? Which type and form would you suggest, and why? What benefits might I get, and how soon? What are my own risks, and how do they compare with not treating? What should I watch for, and when should we review it? **If you are already taking it,** record it in MenoMap (Profile > Medications). MenoMap will show your waves before and after you started it, as a coincidence check, not as proof, so that at the review you have something concrete to talk about. MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing any medicine.

backTranslations.293: Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply prefer other routes. There are many such routes. **Doctor-prescribed options.** Some non-hormonal medicines have evidence of reducing hot flashes. These include some medicines originally made for other conditions, and a new class of medicines made specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them. **Talking and mind-body approaches.** There is evidence that cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied. **Practical changes people find helpful:** layers of clothing that come off quickly; a fan on the desk and by the bed; a cool bedroom and breathable bedding; identifying and reducing your personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this); regular physical activity and a regular sleep routine. **Supplements and herbal products.** For many of these the evidence is mixed or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medicines. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products. **Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own entries before and during a change, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.403: MenoMap is a wellness tracker and information tool. It does not diagnose menopause or any other condition, does not prescribe or change treatment, and does not replace the care of a qualified doctor. backTranslations.416: Most appointments are short, and at that moment it is hard to recall a whole month of nights. People often remember recent days or the worst days. A simple record fills this gap. **What a diary gives your doctor:** how often symptoms happen and how intense they are, not just that they happen; whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same; what was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medicines; if you try a treatment, a starting point for comparison. **Keep it light.** A diary helps only if you keep writing it. MenoMap is built on a one-tap wave button and an evening check-in with four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook. **Two weeks is a good start.** Entries of two to four weeks usually show a clearer picture than one bad week. **Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Appointment tab helps you choose questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479: After 12 months with no period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**, even if it happened only once, and even if it is only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge. In most cases the cause does not turn out to be serious. For example, thinning of the vagina or the lining of the uterus is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat if detected early. This is why public health guidelines say to get it checked instead of waiting. **If you are taking hormone therapy,** some kinds of bleeding may be expected depending on your type of treatment. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual, or at the wrong time should also be checked. **What to do:** Contact your doctor or health service and say you have had bleeding after menopause. Note the date, the amount, and anything you noticed. MenoMap can keep this for you (Profile > Menstrual cycle). MenoMap cannot tell why the bleeding happened. It will remind you to get checked and include it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529: Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints of midlife, and it is rarely due to a single cause. **Night sweats** can wake you straight up, or leave you so hot or damp that you cannot sleep again. **Other common causes:** waking at night to urinate; restlessness or a racing mind; alcohol, which may help you fall asleep but disrupts sleep in the later part of the night; caffeine late in the day; pain, restless legs, or a partner's snoring; snoring or pauses in breathing, which may be a sign of sleep apnoea (it is appropriate to talk about this, especially if you are very sleepy in the day). **What usually helps people.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers of clothing you can remove; a fixed wake-up time; and less alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many doctors can tell you about it. **What to track.** For a week or two note your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and wave log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as context, not as interpretation. **When to get checked.** If poor sleep is affecting your safety (such as when driving), your mood or daily life, or you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night, talk to a doctor.
